cues.en: Welcome back, everyone. Next up, we have Gabriel Gonzalez. Gabriel leads Haskell and Nick's team at Awake Security. He has a blog at Haskellforall.com. I'll link that in the Twitch chat. And his current project of interest is a programmable configuration language named Dal. Gabriel is going to talk to us about marketing Haskell to a mainstream programmer. Take it away, Gabriel. Thank you.
cues.zh: 欢迎回来，各位。接下来是 Gabriel Gonzalez。Gabriel 在 Awake Security 带领 Haskell 和 Nick 的团队。他在 Haskellforall.com 写博客。我会把链接发到 Twitch 聊天里。他目前感兴趣的项目是一个名叫 Dal 的可编程配置语言。Gabriel 将和我们聊聊如何向主流程序员推广 Haskell。交给你了，Gabriel。谢谢。

cues.en: One second. All right. Oops, sorry. Before I begin, I would like to quickly thank the organizers of this conference for making this all possible. And I'm always grateful for the opportunity to meet and also to speak. And today I'm going to be talking about how to market Haskell to mainstream programmers. The inspiration from this talk is a book called Crossing the Chasm, Marketing and Selling High-Tech Products to Mainstream Customers. This book was originally written for startups.
cues.zh: 稍等。好了。哎呀，抱歉。开始之前，我想快速感谢本次会议的组织者，让这一切成为可能。我也一直很感激有机会和大家见面并发言。今天我要讲的是如何向主流程序员推广 Haskell。这个演讲的灵感来自一本书，叫《跨越鸿沟：向主流客户营销和销售高科技产品》。这本书最初是为初创公司写的。

cues.en: But the way I found out about this book was that one of my co-workers was familiar with my passion for evangelizing Haskell, and he saw the connection to the book. So he recommended the book to me. And when I read through it, the book helped crystallize a lot of what I had learned in the course of doing Haskell evangelism and also taught me several new things as well.
cues.zh: 我得知这本书的方式是：我的一位同事知道我很热衷于推广 Haskell，他也看出了这本书和我的关联，于是就把这本书推荐给了我。读完之后，这本书帮我理清了很多在做 Haskell 推广过程中学到的东西，也教会了我一些新东西。

cues.en: So the goal of this talk is to translate the advice in the book to be more relevant for Haskell programmers, or more generally, to be more relevant for people trying to promote new open source technology. This will be my one hot take for the talk. I would like to assert.
cues.zh: 所以这次演讲的目标，是把书中的建议转化得更适合 Haskell 程序员，或者更广泛地说，更适合那些想推广新开源技术的人。这会是我这次演讲里唯一一个犀利观点。我想把它明确提出来。

cues.en: that if you're watching this talk, especially if you're a Haskell developer, there's a very high likelihood that you don't know how to market to mainstream programmers. And that's just because you are a Haskell programmer. That's if there's due to a selection bias in the community. In fact, I'll wager that many people watching this will harbor many misunderstandings about marketing. And my hope is to clear up those misunderstandings in the next few slides.
cues.zh: 如果你在看这个演讲，尤其是如果你是 Haskell 开发者，那很可能你不知道如何向主流程序员做营销。而这只是因为你是 Haskell 程序员。这其实是因为社区中的选择偏差。事实上，我敢打赌，很多看这个演讲的人对营销有很多误解。我希望在接下来几页幻灯片里澄清这些误解。

cues.en: I'm going to use a few concrete examples and I'll use MongoDB as the villain in the upcoming examples with apologies to MongoDB. The first misconception I would like to illustrate is the belief that marketing is about misleading claims. Some people believe that marketing is just about deceiving people or exaggerating a little bit. For example, we might suppose that some developer is contemplating, which database should I select for my business?
cues.zh: 我会用几个具体例子，并且在接下来的例子里把 MongoDB 当作“反派”，这里先向 MongoDB 道个歉。我想说明的第一个误解，是认为营销就是靠误导性宣传。有些人觉得营销不过是骗人，或者稍微夸大一点。比如，我们可以设想某个开发者正在琢磨：我的业务到底该选哪个数据库？

cues.en: And along comes another developer who says, I recommend you use MongoDB, the only database that is web scale, whatever that means. And so people who believe that marketing is about deception will think to themselves, oh, I will steer conversations away from Haskell's poor IDE support. Or more generally, they'll try to exaggerate Haskell's strengths and underplay Haskell's weaknesses. And I call this a misconception because I believe that's not a good thing to do.
cues.zh: 然后又来了一个开发者，他说，我建议你用 MongoDB，唯一一个 web scale 的数据库，管它是什么意思。于是那些认为营销就是欺骗的人就会暗想，哦，我要把话题从 Haskell 糟糕的 IDE 支持上引开。或者更一般地说，他们会夸大 Haskell 的优点，淡化 Haskell 的缺点。我把这称为一种误解，因为我认为这不是什么好事。

cues.en: In fact, I believe it is actually counterproductive. We as a community should be aggressively honest about Haskell's limitations and its downsides. And so the second misconception I would like to address is the belief that marketing is about hype. So there's a belief that the way that a technology becomes mainstream is that first it will generate some hype, which will bring in some new contributors, which will then generate more hype.
cues.zh: 事实上，我认为这其实适得其反。作为社区，我们应该非常坦诚地面对 Haskell 的局限和缺点。我想谈的第二个误解，是认为营销就是炒作。有一种看法是，一项技术走向主流的方式是：先制造一些炒作，吸引来一些新贡献者，然后这些贡献者再带来更多炒作。

cues.en: which will then bring in more contributors. And then that virtuous cycle of hype will eventually take that in the technology mainstream. So for example, again, some developers contemplating to themselves, hmm, how do I know which database is the best one to use? And then some MongoDB evangelists will come along and say, oh, all the cool kids are using MongoDB, hashtag join the convo. And people who believe that marketing is just hype.
cues.zh: 这会带来更多贡献者。然后这种炒作的正向循环最终会把它带入技术主流。比如，又有一些开发者在心里琢磨：嗯，我怎么知道哪个数据库最好用？然后一些 MongoDB 布道者会过来说：哦，所有酷小孩都在用 MongoDB，#join the convo。还有那些认为营销只是炒作的人。

cues.en: We'll then think, oh, I should just spend more time praising Haskell on social media. And that's what's going to get that hype train rolling that will take us mainstream. And I call this a misconception because not only is this not helpful, it's actually harmful. It will actually prevent Haskell from going mainstream. And I'll talk more about why in future slides. The third misconception I would like to address is the belief that marketing is about corporate backing, some way to signal
cues.zh: 然后我们就会想：哦，我该多花点时间在社交媒体上夸 Haskell。这就能让炒作列车开动，把我们带进主流。我称其为误解，因为这不光没帮助，实际上还有害。它实际上会阻碍 Haskell 进入主流。之后的幻灯片里我会多讲讲原因。我想谈的第三个误解是，认为营销就是企业背书，是某种用来表明

cues.en: that a product has financial strength behind it. So for example, some developer might be thinking, maybe I should use Postgres. I've heard great things about it. It's open source and free. It's got a great community behind it. What's not to like? And then along comes somebody who tries to rain on their parade saying, oh MongoDB just raised $150 million in venture capital. If you can't beat them, join them because they're doomed to succeed. And so people who think that marketing is just about a
cues.zh: 产品背后有财务实力。比如，有些开发者可能在想，也许我该用 Postgres。我听过很多它的好评。它开源免费，背后有很棒的社区。有什么可不喜欢的？然后有人跑来泼冷水说：哦，MongoDB 刚融了 1.5 亿美元风险投资。打不过就加入，因为他们注定会成功。所以那些认为营销只是关乎一个

cues.en: show off financial strengths will think that, oh, Facebook adopting Haskell is going to save the language because now we got a big tech company providing full-time developers working on making Haskell better. Or more generally, they think that new technologies need to supplicate in front of large companies to adopt them if they want to go mainstream. And I also consider this a misconception too. And because many startups who the book was originally written for, they have financial backing and they fail to go mainstream. The vast majority of startups fail.
cues.zh: 那些炫耀财力的人会认为，哦，Facebook 采用 Haskell 就能拯救这门语言，因为现在有家大型科技公司提供全职开发者来改进 Haskell。或者更一般地说，他们认为新技术想成为主流，就得在大公司面前乞求被采用。我也认为这是误解。因为这本书最初面向的许多创业公司，它们有资金支持，却没能成为主流。绝大多数创业公司都会失败。

cues.en: So money is not the key bit of the equation that takes you mainstream. So if marketing is not misdeception, and marketing is not hype, and marketing is not corporate backing, then what is marketing? The book provides a really good definition, which I will inline here. And the definition goes like this. It says, marketing is prioritizing the needs of a market, where a market is a group of users that reference each other when making decisions. And there are two
cues.zh: 所以钱并不是让你走向主流的那个关键因素。那么，如果营销不是误导欺骗，营销不是炒作，营销也不是企业背书，那营销是什么？这本书给了一个很好的定义，我在这里直接引用。定义是这样的：营销就是优先考虑一个市场的需求，而市场是一群在做决策时会互相参考的用户。这里有两点

cues.en: things I would like to highlight from that definition. The first is the concept of prioritization. So that means that you make specific decisions not to do something, not to build some feature. So marketing is about what you choose not to build. If you try to do everything, you're not prioritizing at all. You're just spreading yourself in. But it's not just prioritizing needs. It's prioritizing needs of a market. So we might ask ourselves, how big is a market?
cues.zh: 我想从这个定义里强调一下。第一是“优先级”这个概念。也就是说，你要做出具体决定，不去做某件事，不去构建某个功能。所以营销关乎你选择不构建什么。如果你什么都想做，你就根本没有在排优先级，只是在分散精力。但它不只是优先考虑需求，而是优先考虑一个市场的需求。于是我们可能会问自己：一个市场有多大？

cues.en: Is it an individual? No, too small. Is it a company? No, too small. Is it the entire programming community? No, that's too large. So it's somewhere in between there. And a market is a group of users that reference each other. Okay, so these people, they all go to the same conferences. They hire each other.
cues.zh: 它是一个个体吗？不，太小了。它是一家公司吗？不，太小了。它是整个编程社区吗？不，那太大了。所以它介于两者之间。市场就是一群互相引用的用户。好，这些人会参加同样的会议。他们互相招聘。

cues.en: They all tend to hang out on the same subreddits. They will follow each other on social media. They will consult each other when making decisions. They reference each other very heavily. And this group of people is sort of like its own living being. It's got a life of its own. It's this whole that's greater than the sum of the individual people. And so the idea is that if you take the programming community and you break it down into these groups of self-referencing people,
cues.zh: 他们往往混同样的 subreddit。会在社交媒体上互相关注。做决定时会互相咨询。彼此引用非常频繁。这群人有点像自己的生命体。它有自己的生命。它是大于个体之和的整体。所以思路是，如果你把编程社区拆分成这些自我引用的人群，

cues.en: That's called segmentation. And when you prioritize the needs of one of those markets, you're specifically neglecting the needs of other markets. So marketing is about who you choose not to persuade. If you combine those two principles, marketing is kind of the art of saying no, either to potential features or to potential users. And some people think that
cues.zh: 这叫市场细分。当你优先满足其中一个市场的需求时，你就是在刻意忽视其他市场的需求。所以营销的关键在于你选择不去说服谁。把这两条原则结合起来，营销有点像说“不”的艺术——要么对潜在功能说不，要么对潜在用户说不。而有些人认为

cues.en: Marketing is a sleazy thing to do, but I actually firmly believe that marketing is a noble or virtuous task. And the book captures this really well in the following quote. It says, marketing's purpose, therefore, is to develop and shape something that is real and not as people sometimes want to believe, to create illusions. In other words, we are dealing with a discipline more akin to gardening or sculpting than say to spray painting or hypnotism.
cues.zh: 营销是一种不光彩的行为，但我其实坚信，营销是一项高尚或有德行的事业。这本书用下面这句话把这层意思讲得很到位。它说，因此，营销的目的是开发和塑造某种真实的东西，而不是像人们有时愿意相信的那样去制造幻象。换句话说，我们面对的这门学科，更像是在做园艺或雕塑，而不是在喷漆或催眠。

cues.en: So if you do a good job of marketing, you don't need to make misleading claims, you don't need to generate artificial hype, and you don't need corporate backing. But in order to do marketing well, we understand some few basic principles, which brings us to the technology adoption lifecycle. This is a concept that predates the book, and it was created to provide a way to talk about discontinuous changes.
cues.zh: 所以，如果你把营销做好，就不需要做误导性宣传，不需要制造人为炒作，也不需要企业支持。但要把营销做好，我们需要理解少数几条基本原则，这就引出了技术采用生命周期。这个概念早于这本书出现，它的提出是为了提供一种讨论非连续性变化的方式。

cues.en: And you can imagine that if we were to plot all the potential adopters for technology, it might look like a bell curve, where people closer to the left of the bell curve are earlier adopters, and people more the right of the bell curve are later adopters. And the book actually talks about five categories. I've only plotted four. So we'll talk about early adopters and early majority the most. And we won't really talk about the late majority or the laggards.
cues.zh: 你可以想象，如果我们把所有潜在的技术采用者画出来，它可能看起来像一条钟形曲线，越靠近曲线左侧的人越早采用，越靠右的人越晚采用。这本书其实讲了五个类别。我只画了四个。所以我们会重点讲早期采用者和早期大众。我们不会太多讨论后期大众或落后者。

cues.en: As a shorthand, I will use the term visionaries, just like the book, to refer to early adopters. And I will use the term pragmatists to refer to the early majority. Visionaries tend to prefer new technologies. Pragmatists tend to prefer proven technologies. So you'll notice in the diagram that there are little gaps in between each segment of the population. Those gaps represent places where technology adoption can pause or even outright fail.
cues.zh: 为简便起见，我会像书中那样，用“远见者”这个词来指代早期采用者。我也会用“务实者”这个词来指代早期大众。远见者往往偏爱新技术。务实者往往偏爱经过验证的技术。所以你会注意到，图中每个人群细分之间都有小缺口。这些缺口代表技术采用可能停滞、甚至彻底失败的地方。

cues.en: But one of those gaps is much larger than the others, and that it's the gap between early adopters and the early majority. And there are ways that, and so that gap is so large that the book calls it a chasm, and that's why the book is called Crossing the Chasm, because it's trying to help people cross the divide between early adopters and the early majority. And the way you know that you're stuck in the chasm is...
cues.zh: 但这些差距中有一个远大于其他，那就是早期采用者和早期大众之间的差距。这个差距如此之大，以至于书里把它称为鸿沟；这也是这本书叫《跨越鸿沟》的原因，因为它想帮助人们跨越早期采用者和早期大众之间的分界。而判断自己是否困在鸿沟里的方法是……

cues.en: First, there will be an initial burst of enthusiasm and adoption for your technology. And then for some inexplicable reason, adoption will decelerate. It even feels like you've hit a wall unexpectedly, which seems confusing because you would think, you know, maybe strength would build upon strength and then you just keep eventually getting adopted more and more until you get mainstream. But that's not what happens. The second thing you will notice is that visionaries adore you, but pragmatists are suspicious on the best days.
cues.zh: 首先，你的技术会迎来一波最初的热度和采用。然后不知为何，采用速度会慢下来。甚至感觉像是突然撞了墙，这很让人困惑，因为你本以为，势头会不断累积，采用度会越来越高，直到进入主流。但事实并非如此。你会注意到的第二件事是：远见者追捧你，而实用主义者即使在最好的情况下也对你心存疑虑。

cues.en: On the worst days, they may be outright malicious and treat your new technology as the butt-end of a joke. Another important sign is that nothing important ever officially supports you. For example, AWS will release language bindings for their platform. For example, they might create officially supported bindings for C++. Or Java, maybe for Go, I didn't check. But they definitely didn't create it for Haskell. There's no official AWS binding for Haskell.
cues.zh: 在最糟糕的日子里，他们可能会公然地恶意相向，把你的新技术当成笑话的靶子。另一个重要迹象是，从来没有什么重要的东西会正式支持你。比如，AWS 会为他们的平台发布语言绑定。比如，他们可能会为 C++ 创建官方支持的绑定。或者 Java，也许还有 Go，我没查。但他们肯定没有为 Haskell 创建。Haskell 没有官方的 AWS 绑定。

cues.en: So instead, the Haskell community has to pay its own way. We have to create our own binding to AWS, like Amazonica. So that's what it means when we say that nothing important ever officially supports you. And this is something that a lot of people already understood for quite a long time. In fact, Simon Payne and Jones understood this when he gave a talk called A Taste of Haskell, where he described the growth trajectories of several representative languages.
cues.zh: 所以，Haskell 社区只能自力更生。我们必须自己创建到 AWS 的绑定，比如 Amazonica。我们必须自己创建到 AWS 的绑定，比如 Amazonica。所以，当我们说“重要的东西从来不会官方支持你”时，就是这个意思。这是很多人很久以前就已经明白的事情。事实上，Simon Payne and Jones 在名为 A Taste of Haskell 的演讲中就明白这一点，他在演讲中描述了几种代表性语言的增长轨迹。

cues.en: So in the first slide, we show what a successful research language looks like. It grows a little bit and then it fizzles out. And that's fine because the point of a research language is to be a vehicle for research. It doesn't have to go mainstream. And then on the other extreme of the spectrum, we have a language which just keeps growing and growing and growing and growing like a mainstream language. So for example, C++ or Java.
cues.zh: 在第一张幻灯片里，我们展示了一种成功的研究型语言是什么样子。它会发展一阵子，然后逐渐沉寂。这没关系，因为研究型语言的意义就是作为研究的载体。它不必走向主流。而在光谱的另一端，有一种语言会像主流语言一样不断增长、不断增长、不断增长、不断增长。比如 C++ 或 Java。

cues.en: And at some point, it crosses some threshold of immortality, and it joins the pantheon of immortal languages that everybody acknowledges are mainstream. And Simon Payne Jones uses the term, the complete absence of death to describe these languages, because he has such a way with words. So where does Haskell fit in between these two extremes? Well, that brings us to this third slide right here. And this is exactly the growth trajectory you would expect for a language that is stuck in the chasm.
cues.zh: 而在某个时刻，它会跨过某个不朽的门槛，跻身于大家公认的主流不朽语言殿堂。Simon Peyton Jones 用“完全无死亡”这个词来描述这些语言，因为他实在太会措辞了。那么 Haskell 在这两个极端之间处于什么位置呢？这就带我们来到这里的第三张幻灯片。而这正是你预期一个困在鸿沟中的语言会有的增长轨迹。

cues.en: an initial burst of adoption, and then a plateaus. And then, as it eventually picks up in the mainstream, it will grow again. Now, this talk was given about at least 10 years ago. And at the time, he hypothesized that maybe Haskell was starting to break out into the mainstream. But I would firmly contend that Haskell has not yet reached mainstream status, and it's still stuck in the chasm. So why does this chasm exist between visionaries and pragmatists?
cues.zh: 起初采用量激增，随后进入平台期。然后，当它最终在主流中流行起来时，又会再次增长。这场演讲大约是在 10 年前，甚至更早时候做的。当时他推测，Haskell 也许正开始打入主流。但我坚定认为，Haskell 尚未达到主流地位，仍困在鸿沟里。那么，为什么远见者与务实者之间会存在这道鸿沟？

cues.en: Well, the fundamental problem is that visionaries are negative references for pragmatists. And by that we mean that a visionary, when a visionary evangelizes a new technology, it will actually turn off pragmatists from that technology. And why is that? That would seem odd, right? You would think, you know, here us Haskell programmers are trying to exude positive vibes. We're not trying to be mean or turn anybody off yet.
cues.zh: 嗯，根本问题在于，有远见者对实用主义者来说是负面参照。我们的意思是，当一位有远见者去布道一项新技术时，反而会让实用主义者对那项技术敬而远之。为什么呢？这看起来很奇怪，对吧？你会想，我们这些 Haskell 程序员正努力散发正能量。我们并不是想刻薄，也不是想劝退任何人。

cues.en: somehow we're just making them more and more unhappy with us. Well, the fundamental reason is because visionaries and pragmatists have diametrically opposed values. Okay, again, it's not like an extreme, right? There's not like a hard cutoff between visionaries and pragmatists. But let's talk about the values that tend to be associated with each of these two classes of people. So in the next few slides, I'm going to have large walls of text. You don't need to read the whole wall of text. I'm only going to quote
cues.zh: 不知怎么的，我们只是让他们对我们越来越不满意。嗯，根本原因是愿景者和务实者的价值观截然相反。好吧，再说一次，这并不极端，对吧？愿景者和务实者之间并没有硬性分界线。但我们来谈谈这两类人各自往往关联的价值观。所以在接下来几页幻灯片里，我会放一大段一大段的文字。你不需要读完整整一大段文字。我只会引用

cues.en: the parts highlighted in bold. If you'd like to read the full text later, I will share my slides and there'll also be a link on the last slide. So for people viewing the recording, they can get the link as well. All right, so back to the slides. The first difference between visionaries and pragmatists is that visionaries have a lack of respect for the value of their colleagues' experiences. And the book puts it like this. Visionaries
cues.zh: 加粗高亮的部分。如果之后想读全文，我会分享我的幻灯片，最后一页上也会有链接。所以看录像的人也能拿到链接。好，回到幻灯片。愿景者和务实者的第一个区别是，愿景者不重视同事经验的价值。书里是这样说的。愿景者

cues.en: do not expect to be buying a well-tested product with an extensive list of industry references. Instead, if such a reference base exists, it may actually turn them off, indicating that for this technology at any rate, they are already too late. Pragmatists, on the other hand, deeply value the experience of their colleagues. And this is a perfect example of why their values are diametrically opposed.
cues.zh: 不要指望买到一款经过充分测试、拥有大量行业参考案例的产品。相反，如果这样的参考案例库已经存在，反而可能让他们望而却步，说明对这项技术来说，他们无论如何都已经太晚了。另一方面，务实主义者非常看重同事的经验。这正好说明了为什么他们的价值观截然相反。

cues.en: So for technology, the fewer references something has, the more visionaries like it, because they think to themselves, oh, I got it on the ground floor for this new technology. For primitives, it's the opposite. The more references a technology has, the more they like it. But that's not the only difference between them. Here's another. Visionaries take a greater interest in technology than in their own industry. And the book puts it like this. Visionaries are bored.
cues.zh: 所以，对技术来说，某个东西被引用得越少，有远见的人反而越喜欢它，因为他们会想：哦，这项新技术我刚起步时就入场了。对原语来说，正好相反。一项技术被引用得越多，他们越喜欢。但这还不是它们之间唯一的区别。还有一个区别是：有远见的人对技术本身的兴趣，大过对自己行业的兴趣。书里是这么说的：有远见的人会感到厌倦。

cues.en: with the mundane details of their own industries. They like to talk and think high-tech. Pragmatists, on the other hand, don't put a lot of stake in futuristic things. And if you didn't know that this book was written about startups, you'd think, gosh, that is a perfect description of the differences between, you know, the stereotypical Haskell programmer and the stereotypical, say, Go programmer. You got the Haskell programmer who is, you know, the architecture astronaut, wants to talk about, you know, profunctor optics.
cues.zh: 以及自己行业里那些平淡琐碎的细节。他们喜欢谈高科技，也喜欢用高科技来思考。而实用主义者则不太看重那些未来感十足的东西。如果你不知道这本书写的是创业公司，你会想：天哪，这简直完美描述了刻板印象中的 Haskell 程序员和刻板印象中的、比如说，Go 程序员之间的区别。你瞧，Haskell 程序员就是那种，你知道，架构宇航员，总想聊什么 profunctor optics。

cues.en: On the other hand, you got your stereotypical Go programmer who's like, I can write a web server in any language. What's the point of learning something new like Haskell? But the differences keep going. This is not the only difference between visionaries and pragmatists. For example, visionaries fail to recognize the importance of existing product infrastructure. They do not expect to find components for these systems lying around. Whereas pragmatists, when they see visionaries going their own route, they shudder.
cues.zh: 另一方面，你也有那种刻板印象里的 Go 程序员，他会说：我用任何语言都能写 Web 服务器。那学 Haskell 这种新东西有什么意义？但差异还不止这些。这并不是愿景派和务实派之间唯一的区别。比如，愿景派认识不到现有产品基础设施的重要性。他们不指望这些系统的组件能现成找到。而务实派看到愿景派走自己的路时，会不寒而栗。

cues.en: Okay, so pragmatists want everything to be ready to go out of the box. They don't want to do it themselves. And the final difference is that visionaries are just overall disruptive people. They create a lot of work for themselves, for their co-workers, for their company, for their industry. They are the kind of people who like to rock the boat. As the book puts it, from a pragmatist point of view, visionaries are the people who come in and soak up all the budget for their projects.
cues.zh: 好吧，务实主义者希望一切都开箱即用。他们不想自己动手。最后一个区别是，远见者总体上就是一群爱颠覆的人。他们会给自己、同事、公司乃至行业制造大量工作。他们就是那种喜欢打破现状的人。正如书中所说，从务实主义者的角度看，远见者就是那些跑进来、把项目预算全吸干的人。

cues.en: If the project is a success, they take all the credit. While a pragmatist gets stuck trying to maintain a system that is so state of the art, no one is quite sure how to keep it working. Pragmatists, on the other hand, tend to be committed long term to their profession and the company at which they work. They are very cautious about grandiose schemes because they know they will have to live with the results. All right, so suppose you believe me that visionaries and pragmatists have diametrically opposed values. How can we overcome that?
cues.zh: 如果项目成功，功劳全归他们。而务实者却困在维护一个如此前沿的系统上，没人完全确定该怎么让它继续运转。另一方面，务实者往往长期投入自己的职业和所在公司。他们对宏大的计划非常谨慎，因为他们知道自己得承受结果。好，那么假设你相信我说远见者和务实者的价值观完全对立。我们该怎么克服这一点？

cues.en: After all, we just said that the more we visionaries evangelize it to new technology, the worse that makes things get. And so you might think, okay, if I can't evangelize something, maybe I'll just make it so good that if I build it, they will come. But the problem is that it can be really hard to build something that good. We certainly don't want to sell out to some VC funded startup or to some consulting company and give them too large of a stake in our ecosystem and too much influence.
cues.zh:
毕竟，我们刚说过，我们这些有远见的人越是向新技术布道，事情反而越糟。
所以你可能会想：好吧，如果我不能布道某个东西，也许我就把它做得足够好，做到“我建好了，他们自然会来”。
但问题是，要把东西做到那么好真的很难。
我们当然不想投靠某个风投支持的初创公司或咨询公司，给他们在我们生态里过大的股份和过多的话语权。

cues.en: We don't want to burn out working late nights and weekends trying to make pragmatists happy, especially when they don't even like us. Why are we going to spend a lot of time trying to please people who hate us? Well, I don't think we actually, I don't think we need to sell out and I don't think we need to burn out. We don't need to work harder, but we do need to work smarter. And in order to do that, we need to understand what is the fundamental difference between pragmatists and visionaries. And the fundamental difference is that
cues.zh: 我们不想为了讨好务实派而熬夜加班、周末也干活，最后把自己累垮，尤其他们根本不喜欢我们。为什么要花大量时间去取悦讨厌我们的人？其实我觉得，我们不需要出卖自己，也不需要把自己累垮。我们不需要更拼命，而是需要更聪明地工作。要做到这一点，就得理解务实派和愿景派的根本区别。而根本区别在于：

cues.en: Visionaries are project oriented and pragmatists are market oriented. And what that means is that when a visionary evaluates a new tool, they ask themselves, is this tool the best choice for the specific project that I'm working on? And for example, they ask, is this the right tool for the job? And if they move to a new project, they'll reevaluate their tools. And for many people listening to this, you don't think to themselves, well, of course that's the way you evaluate tools. Is there any other way to do it?
cues.zh: 愿景派以项目为导向，务实派以市场为导向。这意味着，愿景派评估新工具时会问自己：这个工具是我当前这个具体项目的最佳选择吗？比如他们会问：这是适合这项工作的工具吗？如果换到新项目，他们会重新评估工具。对很多听众来说，你会想：当然是这样评估工具啊，还能有别的办法吗？

cues.en: But it turns out that there is, because pragmatists think in a different way. Pragmatists, when they evaluate a new tool, they ask themselves, is this tool the best one for my industry? They tend to be very herd oriented, partly because they're risk averse, and partly because they want to take advantage of economies of scale for their entire industry adopting a tool. So if we want to get through to pragmatists, we need to start thinking, speaking, and building
cues.zh: 但事实证明是有的，因为务实派的思考方式不同。务实派在评估新工具时会问自己：这个工具对我的行业来说是最好的吗？他们往往非常从众，部分原因是规避风险，部分原因是希望借助整个行业采用某工具所带来的规模经济。所以，如果我们想打动务实派，就需要开始思考、表达和构建

cues.en: in a market-oriented way in order to persuade them. That's why the discipline is called marketing. So we need to stop focusing on individual people's needs and start focusing on the needs of markets, these groups of self-referencing users. And one of the reasons that we want to persuade pragmatists, despite the fact that they can be so standoffish at first, is because
cues.zh: 以市场为导向的方式，才能说服他们。这就是为什么这门学科叫市场营销。所以我们需要停止关注个体需求，开始关注市场的需求，也就是这些自我参照的用户群体。我们想说服务实派的原因之一——尽管他们起初可能很冷淡——是因为

cues.en: They may be hard to win over, but when you do, they become your greatest ally. In fact, they will actually be greater allies than the early adopters. The book has this great quote. The only thing we need to do is replace the word startup with new technology. And the quote goes like this. Once a new technology has earned its spurs with the pragmatist buyers within a given market, they tend to be very loyal to it, and they even go out of their way to help it succeed. In fact,
cues.zh: 他们可能很难被争取过来，但一旦你赢得他们，他们就会成为你最有力的盟友。事实上，他们会比早期采用者更有力。书里有句很棒的话。我们只需把 startup 这个词换成新技术。原话是这样的：一旦一项新技术在特定市场赢得了实用主义买家的认可，他们往往会对它非常忠诚，甚至会不遗余力地帮它成功。事实上，

cues.en: they will actually defend the technology fiercely against competitors once they've embraced it. And the reason why is because pragmatists are market oriented. When they adopt a tool, they're not adopting it on behalf of themselves. They feel like they're adopting it on behalf of their industry. So they have this very strong desire to make any new tool that they adopt official or standard for their industry. And they will try to protect its status as the official or standard tool once they adopt it.
cues.zh: 一旦他们接纳了这项技术，他们就会坚决捍卫它、对抗竞争对手。原因在于，实用主义者是以市场为导向的。他们采用一个工具时，并不是代表自己采用。他们觉得自己是在代表整个行业采用它。所以他们有很强烈的愿望，想让自己采用的任何新工具成为行业的官方或标准工具。而且一旦采用，他们就会努力保护它作为官方或标准工具的地位。

cues.en: All right, so suppose that I've persuaded you that you want to convince pragmatists to adopt your tool. We still don't know how to do that. And because we've already identified kind of a chicken and egg problem, pragmatists are risk averse and they want references. As the book puts it, how can you accumulate the number of references the pragmatist requires when virtually everyone left a call on is also pragmatists? It's like a chicken and egg problem. How do you kickstart that cycle of positive references?
cues.zh: 好吧，假设我已经说服你：你想说服实用主义者采用你的工具。但我们还是不知道怎么做到这一点。而且因为我们已经识别出一种先有鸡还是先有蛋的问题——实用主义者厌恶风险，他们想要推荐。正如书里所说，当你几乎要拜访的每个人也都是实用主义者时，你如何积累实用主义者所需数量的推荐？这就像一个鸡生蛋、蛋生鸡的问题。你如何启动这个正面推荐的循环？

cues.en: Well it turns out there is a recipe for breaking that for generating that cycle of positive references. I'll call it the recipe for success. It's an oversimplification of what's in the book but I think it's an okay distillation. So the first step is that we need to solve an enormous problem and the problem has to be so bad that a few pragmatists have to use your tool because remember pragmatists are risk averse
cues.zh: 事实证明，确实有一套方法能打破这种局面，形成正向推荐循环。我把它叫作“成功配方”。这是对书里内容的过度简化，但我觉得还算是个不错的提炼。第一步是，我们需要解决一个巨大的问题，而且这个问题必须严重到让一些务实派不得不用你的工具，因为要记住，务实派是厌恶风险的。

cues.en: and they're not going to use a tool without references unless they absolutely have to. So, for example, the pragmatists will think to themselves, you know, I'd rather not try something new, but I have to use a Haskell in anger. But it's not enough to force them to use your tool. You can get a couple of them to do that, but after that experience, they will not necessarily refer your tool to their pragmatist colleagues.
cues.zh: 除非绝对必要，否则他们不会用一个没有推荐背书的工具。所以举个例子，务实派会心里想：你知道，我宁愿不尝试新东西，但我不得不在实际项目里用 Haskell。但强迫他们用你的工具还不够。你能让几个人这么做，但在那之后，他们未必会把你的工具推荐给同样是务实派的同事。

cues.en: So that leads us to the second step, which is that you have to provide a best-in-class experience. It's not enough to be good, you have to be the best for that market. You don't need to be the best for the entire programming community, because everybody in the programming community has different needs, and that's basically impossible. But at least for the industry that that pragmatists care about, you have to be the best. So when those few pragmatists are forced to try Haskell, they need to walk away from that thinking to themselves, wow!
cues.zh: 所以这就引出了第二步：你必须提供一流的体验。光好还不够，你必须成为那个市场里最好的。你不需要成为整个编程社区里最好的，因为编程社区里每个人都有不同的需求，这基本上不可能。但至少对于实用主义者关心的那个行业，你必须做到最好。所以当那少数实用主义者被迫尝试 Haskell 时，他们离开时得在心里想：哇！

cues.en: Haskell is way better than I thought. It blows away the competition. Now that's easier said than done, right? If we could build something like that, wouldn't we have done it already? Actually, I would say that a lot of people don't know how to do that. And so the first step along the way to being able to build a best-in-class tool is to focus your effort on one market at a time, because there's no way you can build a top-notch experience otherwise.
cues.zh:
Haskell 比我以为的强多了。
它把竞争对手远远甩开了。
不过，说起来容易做起来难，对吧？
如果我们真能做出那样的东西，不早就做出来了吗？
其实，我得说很多人并不知道该怎么做。
所以，要打造一流的工具，第一步就是一次只聚焦一个市场，因为否则你根本不可能做出顶尖的体验。

cues.en: And that means that doing so may lead to neglecting other industries, but pragmatists will not alter you for that. Quite the opposite. Pragmatists would actually prefer if you tell them Haskell is not good for X, because if you tell them Haskell is okay for X and they try it and they have a bad time, then they actually turn into a negative reference. You actually would prefer that they just don't try it at all until it's ready. So pragmatists will just think themselves, you know, Haskell may not be a good fit for other industries, but...
cues.zh: 这意味着这样做可能会忽视其他行业，但务实主义者不会因此怪你。恰恰相反。务实主义者其实更希望你直接告诉他们 Haskell 不适合 X；因为如果你说 Haskell 做 X 还行，他们试了之后体验很差，就会变成负面参考。你其实更希望他们在 Haskell 准备好之前根本别去试。所以务实主义者只会自己想：Haskell 可能确实不太适合其他行业，但……

cues.en: I'm okay with that. It doesn't have to be everything to everybody. So to summarize that recipe, I like to create what's called the perfect pitch, where if you can say this truthfully, then Haskell has gone mainstream. So you should be able to say Haskell is the best tool for some industry. Everybody's saying great things about it. Ask your colleagues if you don't believe me.
cues.zh: 我对此没意见。它不必对所有人都是全部。那么总结一下这个配方，我喜欢打造所谓的“完美推介”：如果你能如实说出这句话，那就说明 Haskell 已经主流化了。所以你应该能说，Haskell 是某个行业里最好的工具。大家都在夸它。不信我的话，就去问问你的同事。

cues.en: Notice that this pitch has absolutely no appeal to the technical merit of Haskell whatsoever. It's purely a references-oriented appeal. And if you work backwards from that pitch, that will help you better understand what you need to do to make it true. And I want to really reiterate the importance of focusing on one market, and I'm going to use an extended analogy to make that point. And so the analogy I'm going to use is going to be like a nuclear chain reaction.
cues.zh: 注意，这个推介完全没有诉诸 Haskell 的技术优势。它纯粹是靠推荐/口碑来打动人。如果你从这个推介倒推，就能更好地理解你需要做什么才能让它成真。我想再次强调聚焦单一市场的重要性，并且我会用一个展开的类比来说明这一点。我要用的这个类比，会类似核链式反应。

cues.en: And I'm not a nuclear physicist, so I'm probably greatly oversimplifying things. But my very rough understanding is that when a nuclear reaction has some of these various reactive particles, and if they reach a critical mass, then the reaction goes out of control. You have a chain reaction. That would be like the adoption of a tool growing uncontrollably. This is what Simon Payne Jones would call the complete absence of death. And if the reaction is subcritical, meaning that you just don't have enough positive references to kickstart things,
cues.zh: 我不是核物理学家，所以很可能把问题大大简化了。但我的粗略理解是：当核反应中有一些这类反应性粒子，并且它们达到临界质量时，反应就会失控，形成链式反应。这就像某个工具的采用率不受控制地增长。Simon Payne Jones 会把这种情况称为“死亡的完全缺席”。而如果反应是次临界的，也就是说你没有足够多的正面推荐来启动它，

cues.en: then eventually things, the reaction will just fizzle out. The tool adoption will slowly fade away. And this is what Simon Payne Jones calls the slow death. And people already intuitively understand this, but they try to manufacture artificial hype to stimulate the reaction. And that doesn't work because primitives are very hard to fool. They can see through it. But if we understand how, if we think in terms of markets, then we can actually make it easier to kickstart such a chain reaction.
cues.zh: 那么最终反应就会逐渐熄灭，工具的采用也会慢慢消退。这就是 Simon Payne Jones 所说的“缓慢死亡”。人们其实凭直觉已经理解这一点，但他们试图制造人为炒作来刺激反应。这行不通，因为原语很难被糊弄，它们能看穿。但如果我们理解其中的机制，如果我们从市场的角度来思考，就其实可以让这种链式反应更容易被启动。

cues.en: So let's use this little diagram right here, where these squares, you can think of these squares as reaction chambers. And a positive reference denoted by these white circles would be like a reactive particle. And then if two positive references collide, then they will react and generate more positive references. For example, the way this might manifest is some organization will take a chance on your tool.
cues.zh: 我们就用这里这张小示意图，你可以把这些方块看作反应腔。白色圆圈表示的正向推荐，就像反应粒子。两个正向推荐相撞，就会发生反应，产生更多正向推荐。比如，这种情况的一种体现是：某个组织愿意冒险试用你的工具。

cues.en: And then it works out, so then new developers are trained, and then contributions are made back to the ecosystem, and then standards are drafted, and more positive references are created. Great. That represents the amplification of the positive reaction. Vice versa, we can have negative references, which will represent as black dots. And if a positive and negative reference collide, then maybe they fizzle out. This is an oversimplification, but you get the idea. All right, now here's the key bit where markets come in.
cues.zh: 然后它就行得通了：新开发者得到培养，贡献回馈到生态，标准被起草，更多正向引用被创建。很好。这代表了正向反应的放大。反过来，也会有负向引用，用黑点表示。如果正向和负向引用相撞，它们可能就彼此抵消了。这是过度简化，但你明白意思。好，接下来是关键部分：市场从哪里介入。

cues.en: All right, so the programming community at large is not one giant reaction chamber. Instead, you can think of each market as being its own isolated reaction chamber. That means that positive references tend to stay within their own market. Negative references also tend to stay within their own market. And this is because we're going back to the definition of a market.
cues.zh: 总的来说，编程社区并不是一个巨大的反应室。相反，你可以把每个市场看作各自独立的反应室。这意味着正面引用往往留在自己的市场内。负面引用也往往留在自己的市场内。这是因为我们要回到市场的定义。

cues.en: where a market is a group of users that reference each other. That's why references tend to stay within the respective markets. And so we can use that fact to kickstart the chain reaction more easily. First, let's illustrate how we would not do it. So let's suppose that there were three potential markets that Haskell could target to go mainstream. Maybe there's data science, then there's finance, and then there's interpreters.
cues.zh: 市场是一群相互引用的用户。这就是为什么引用往往留在各自的市场内。因此，我们可以利用这一点更容易地启动连锁反应。首先，我们来说明不该怎么做。假设 Haskell 有三个潜在市场可以瞄准以走向主流。也许有数据科学，然后是金融，然后是解释器。

cues.en: and they're mostly isolated from one another. And if we do, if we just spread ourselves thin and try to do a little bit good of a job for each one of these markets, then we never kickstart a chain reaction because we never reach a critical density of positive references to trigger that amplification that we're looking for. But now suppose that we were to focus a little bit more on interpreters.
